newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh T-bills resume, market attractive but small.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh T-bills resume, market attractive but small.

text.p: Kazakhstan auctioned six and three-month treasury bills (GKOs) on Monday and Tuesday, dispelling uncertainty prompted after the former Soviet republic stopped issuing debt last month.

The Finance Ministry suspended T-bill auctions in December for three weeks, saying it had enough cash to cover immediate budget needs from a $200 million Eurobond issue that was snapped up on international markets last month.
But three, six and 12-month GKOs, whose annual yields average some 30 percent, will be used again this year to shore up state coffers and attract foreign investment.
Foreign investors say Kazakh paper is attractive but active buying is thwarted by limits on foreign participation at auctions and the small size of the secondary market.

"It is true, the $200 million was enough to finance the state's most urgent expenses," Oleg Tsurkan, chief dealer at Dutch bank ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Kazakhstan, told Reuters. "But now a new budget is being implemented, so more GKO issues are sure to follow."
ABN AMRO led the oil-rich Central Asian republic's three year Eurobond debut in December, priced to yield 9.3 percent or 350 basis points above comparable U.S. Treasury notes.
While analysts cannot say when a new Eurobond issue might follow, Kazakhstan is under pressure to implement a tight 1997 budget, with a deficit set at 3.16 percent of gross domestic product.
"According to my information, GKOs are expected to bring in some $180 million this year to help cover the budget gap," Tsurkan said.
Foreign investors have displayed keen interest in Kazakh GKOs and take part in auctions, but more active investment in state securities is thwarted by two main factors.
First, foreign investors are allowed to buy only 10 to 20 percent of each issue.
"This is not quite in compliance with free market rules," Tsurkan admits. "But the state wants to back local banks."
The other is the small size of the secondary market in Kazakh debt.

"Foreign investors are much less limited when dealing on the secondary market," said Eric Fine, London-based Russia and Eastern Europe debt strategist at bankers Morgan Stanley and Co International Ltd. "The only real constriction is the small size of the market."
Tsurkan estimated the volume of GKOs circulating on the secondary market at about $80 to $85 million.
"This figure is very close to mine," said Fine. "The market is just too small, but it remains attractive."
